records.title: Sands of Time
records.location: Mekong River in Vietnam; Cambodia (national parks, per the article); the article is otherwise global
records.summary: A global feature on sand mining and the construction industry. For the Mekong basin, it states that '55 million tons of sand is mined from the Mekong River in Vietnam each year, which has lowered the level of the river by three feet', and, citing a World Wildlife Fund report, links this to salt-water intrusion, coastal erosion and pressure on fish stocks that 'feed over 60 million people'. It says Cambodia, Vietnam, Malaysia and Indonesia have banned sand exports to Singapore, that sand mining in Cambodian national parks has killed mangroves and sea grasses, and that Vietnam 'may run out of sand for domestic use alone by 2020'. Most of the article covers other regions (India, China's Poyang Lake, Indonesia, Singapore, Dubai, the US) and solutions such as recycling and alternative materials.
records.limitations: Mekong content is brief and secondhand (WWF report, author Vince Beiser, other interviewees); figures are not independently verified or dated in the article. The article is mostly non-Mekong. Poyang Lake and Yangtze are outside the basin. Automated English summary; native-language review may be needed.

records.title: How the scramble for sand is destroying the Mekong
records.originalTitle: How the scramble for sand is destroying the Mekong
records.location: Lower Mekong River and Mekong Delta, Cambodia and Vietnam
records.summary: BBC News reports that sand extraction from the Mekong riverbed in Cambodia and Vietnam is driven by global demand. It says "half a million people are at risk of losing their homes" as banks collapse. River scientist Prof Stephen Darby is quoted as saying studies on the lower Mekong show the bed has been lowered by several metres in a few years over many hundreds of kilometres. The article cites WWF and the Mekong River Commission as saying the bed of the two main Mekong Delta channels "lost 1.4m in elevation in the 10 years to 2008", and that "between two and three metres have been lost in elevation since 1990". It cites research in Nature saying sand mining on one 20km stretch is "non-sustainable". It notes Vietnam and Cambodia officially banned Mekong sand exports in 2009 and 2017 respectively, yet Mekong sand is advertised online in orders of 20,000 to 200,000 tonnes. Prof Rolf Aalto reportedly found that Singapore continues to record imports from Cambodia although Cambodia claims not to export. The Cambodian ministry did not respond to BBC's request for comment. Experts quoted call for better data and governance.
records.limitations: News article; figures are attributed to cited experts, organisations and studies and are not independently verified. No specific location or river stretch is named beyond the lower Mekong and Mekong Delta. Global figures are not Mekong-specific. Cambodia's export claims are not answered by the ministry. Automated English summary; native-language review may be needed.

reviews.reviewReason: The article is a global feature, but it contains an explicit, attributed passage tying sand mining to the Mekong River in Vietnam: "55 million tons of sand is mined from the Mekong River in Vietnam each year, which has lowered the level of the river by three feet." It also cites a WWF report on salt-water intrusion, coastal erosion and fish stocks, and says sand mining in Cambodian national parks killed mangroves and sea grasses. Date evidence is the publisher metadata 2019-10-06T19:00:04+00:00. The article is not about gold mining; gold is mentioned only as a comparison. Weaknesses: the Mekong content is brief and secondhand, and the draft's originalTitle "Sands of Time | Atmos" cannot be checked against the supplied text, which shows only "Sands of Time" at the end. The draft title is a faithful match for that. The Cambodia claim is not tied to the Mekong basin in the text, so it is a weaker basis. Vietnam is supported by the Mekong passage. No same-incident duplicate exists in the archive; the WWF report records are different documents.

reviews.reviewReason: The BBC article substantively covers sand extraction and dredging on the Mekong in Cambodia and Vietnam. Scope quote 'Extracted from the bed of this giant river in Cambodia and Vietnam, sand is one of the Earth's most sought-after resources' appears verbatim and ties the topic to the basin. The title and original title match exactly (English source). The date '19 December 2019' appears in the body and matches publisher metadata. It is not about gold mining. The figures in the draft (1.4m in 10 years to 2008, 2-3m since 1990, 20km stretch, 2009/2017 export bans, 20,000-200,000 tonnes) are all supported by quotes and attributed. No nearby archive record covers this same BBC article, so no duplicate. Minor caveats: the draft summary's 'half a million people' claim is an unattributed article statement, and the Prof Aalto finding is attributed correctly.
